reading.rtitle: Two segments, one budget -- the note that goes to the board
paras: The two segments do not look alike on any line. The distributor segment is much bigger in volume: it moves about four times as many litres as the workshop segment, and it always has. It is also the easier of the two to serve, because everything goes out in full loads and nothing has to be explained twice.

The margin tells a different story. The workshop segment is the more profitable of the two by a wide distance, and the gap has been getting wider, not narrower, for three years. Coverage is the reason. We reach fewer than one workshop in five, so almost every new workshop is a first sale rather than a bigger one, and first sales carry the best margin we have.

The benchmark is uncomfortable. Our largest competitor reaches nearly twice as many workshops as we do and is growing faster in that segment than in any other. In the distributor ranking we are second and comfortable. In the workshop ranking we are fifth. The most efficient use of next year's budget is not the segment where we are strongest. It is the one where we are furthest behind.
reading.source: Simulated internal note, written for this lesson -- not a published document

listenings.text: I am going to give you the comparison in three numbers, because three is all anybody remembers. Number one, volume. The distributor segment is about four times bigger than the workshop segment, and it is easier to serve. Number two, margin. The workshop segment is far more profitable, and the gap between the two has been getting wider every year for three years. Number three, and this is the uncomfortable one, coverage. We reach fewer than one workshop in five. Our largest competitor reaches nearly twice as many as we do. So the honest summary is this. We are second in the segment where we are comfortable and fifth in the segment where the money is. I would rather be third in the second one than second in the first one, and that is the recommendation.

The most common mistake I see with comparison is that people compare the thing that is easiest to measure instead of the thing that decides. Volume is easy. Everybody has volume. So the slide shows volume, the room discusses volume, and the decision gets made on volume, and nobody notices that volume was never the question. Ask yourself one thing before you build the chart. If this number moved twenty per cent tomorrow, would the decision change? If the answer is no, the number is decoration. It is very good decoration. It fills a slide beautifully and it costs somebody a week of work. And one more rule, which sounds obvious and almost nobody follows it. Never compare two things on a chart unless you are prepared to say which one you would choose. A comparison without a recommendation is homework you handed to the room.
